prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "T-Mobile US, Inc." (ticker TMUS), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "TMUS", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: T-Mobile US, Inc.
markets: US postpaid wireless phone and data plans
Home broadband (5G fixed wireless and fiber through joint ventures)
Mobile devices and accessories sold on installment plans
Business and government wireless and connectivity
Wholesale network access for other brands and satellite-to-phone service (T-Satellite)

mission.statement: to be the best in the world at connecting customers to their world
mission.source: T-Mobile press release on T-Satellite, June 23, 2025 ("As part of T-Mobile's mission to be the best in the world at connecting customers to their world")
mission.plain: T-Mobile wants to keep people connected to everything they care about, better than anyone else.

about.plain: T-Mobile runs one of the three big mobile phone networks in the United States. People pay it every month so their phones can call, text and use the internet. It also sells phones and offers home internet that comes through the air from its cell towers. It had about 142 million customers at the end of 2025.
about.customers: Families, individuals, businesses and government agencies across the US pay it for phone plans, home internet and devices.
about.everyday: If your phone says T-Mobile or Metro at the top of the screen, your calls and videos travel over its towers.

money.part: Monthly phone and home internet plans (postpaid)
money.plain: monthly bills for phone lines, watches, tablets and 5G home internet
selling phones, often paid over 24 months
pay-in-advance plans like Metro by T-Mobile
renting its network to other phone brands
fiber-to-the-home through joint ventures such as Metronet
texting and some apps from space where towers do not reach

result.summary: T-Mobile has a solid competitive advantage built on scale and spectrum: the 2020 Sprint merger gave it a large lead in mid-band 5G spectrum, and it now wins most independent network awards (Ookla, Opensignal, P3, J.D. Power network quality) while still being seen as the value 'Un-carrier'. In a three-player national market with huge spectrum and network costs, that position is hard to copy, though cable companies selling cheap mobile plans and rising churn show it is not unassailable.

pricingPower.evidence: It raised legacy plan prices by $5 a line from April 2025 and lifted a monthly fee from April 23, 2025, and postpaid ARPA rose 2% to $152.91 in Q2 2026, but postpaid phone churn climbed to 1.02% in Q4 2025 and postpaid account churn rose to 0.99% in Q2 2026 from 0.92% a year earlier.

moats.evidence: The magenta 'Un-carrier' brand is widely known for value and customer-friendly moves, and it reported a record wireless NPS of 46 in Q2 2026 (HarrisX), but fee increases have dented that image.
Device installment plans, 24-month bill credits on phone deals and family and home-internet bundles make leaving costly, though number porting keeps switching easy in principle.
Customers on any US network can call and text each other, so more T-Mobile users do not make the service more valuable to others; more users only add data that helps network planning.

With 142.4 million customers at the end of 2025 and $33,924M of core adjusted EBITDA, it spreads its roughly $10B a year of network capital across a huge base, letting it lead on network quality while still pricing for value.

Only three companies (T-Mobile, Verizon, AT&T) run national US mobile networks, because spectrum ($98,032M of spectrum licenses on its balance sheet) and nationwide towers are too costly for new entrants, as EchoStar's 2025 spectrum sales showed.
Its Un-carrier moves since 2013 (ending contracts, including taxes and fees, free satellite texting on top plans) forced rivals to follow, but most have now been copied.

It built the first nationwide standalone 5G network and integrated Sprint and UScellular quickly, showing strong network-deployment and integration skill, though rivals have similar engineering capabilities.

Its deep mid-band spectrum (notably the 2.5 GHz band from Sprint) gives it capacity and speed advantages that rivals cannot easily buy, reflected in $98,032M of spectrum licenses at December 31, 2025.

customers.evidence: It reported a record wireless NPS of 46 in Q2 2026 (HarrisX), the highest it says for any big-three carrier, and full-year 2025 postpaid phone churn of 0.93%, though churn rose to 1.02% in Q4 2025 and account churn to 0.99% in Q2 2026.

talent.evidence: It appeared on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For list in 2018-2021 and 2024 and has about 75,000 employees, but store closures and a push to become 'AI-enabled, digital-first' bring job changes.

product.evidence: Ookla named it Best Mobile Network in the US for H2 2025 and H1 2026, Opensignal gave it every overall experience award, P3 named it Test Champion in Q2 2026, and J.D. Power ranked it highest for network quality in five of six regions in its 2026 study, ending a 35-report run of rival wins.

competitors.name: Verizon Communications
competitors.note: National wireless carrier competing for postpaid phone and fixed wireless home internet customers, now pushing for volume growth under CEO Dan Schulman.

competitors.name: AT&T
competitors.note: National wireless carrier bundling mobile with fiber broadband, plus business and FirstNet public-safety service.

competitors.name: Comcast (Xfinity Mobile)
competitors.note: Cable broadband and fast-growing mobile service on Verizon's network, sold as cheap bundles.

competitors.name: Charter Communications (Spectrum, including Cox)
competitors.note: Cable broadband and Spectrum Mobile on Verizon's network; competes with T-Mobile's 5G home internet.

competitors.name: EchoStar (Boost Mobile)
competitors.note: Small wireless carrier now relying more on partner networks after selling spectrum in 2025.

competitors.name: Altice USA (Optimum)
competitors.note: Cable broadband and Optimum Mobile in the Northeast and other regions.

competitors.name: SpaceX (Starlink)
competitors.note: Satellite broadband competing with 5G home internet in rural areas, and T-Mobile's partner for T-Satellite direct-to-cell service.

marketShare.market: Share of Q2 2026 US wireless phone/line net additions among the five largest providers (Verizon, AT&T, Comcast, Charter as reported; T-Mobile is a Recon Analytics estimate because it no longer reports phone net additions)

threats: Cable companies (Comcast, Charter-Cox) adding hundreds of thousands of cheap bundled mobile lines a quarter on Verizon's network
Verizon's shift under Dan Schulman to win back market share and AT&T's fiber-plus-wireless bundles
Rising churn after price and fee increases (postpaid phone churn 1.02% in Q4 2025; account churn 0.99% in Q2 2026 vs 0.92%) and slowing account growth (Q2 2026 net account adds down 13% to 277,000)
A mature US wireless market where growth mostly comes from taking rivals' customers
Heavy debt (about $84.6 billion of short- and long-term debt at June 30, 2026 against $2.8 billion of cash)
Satellite direct-to-phone services and spectrum moves by SpaceX could reshape rural coverage and competition
Execution risk in the UScellular integration (closed August 1, 2025), fiber joint ventures and a CEO transition (Srini Gopalan since November 1, 2025)

ceo.name: Srini Gopalan
ceo.background: St. Stephen's College (Delhi University) graduate and IIM Ahmedabad postgraduate in management; worked at Unilever, Accenture, Capital One, T-Mobile UK, Vodafone and Bharti Airtel, ran Deutsche Telekom's German business, and was T-Mobile US COO from March 2025 before becoming CEO on November 1, 2025

c1.evidence: US wireless is a mature industry; T-Mobile leads on network quality and customer growth, but service revenue grew about 9% in Q2 2026, not the pace of an emerging industry.

c2.evidence: Customers choose it for a network that now wins Ookla, Opensignal, P3 and J.D. Power awards combined with Un-carrier value perks, an edge rooted in mid-band spectrum that rivals cannot easily copy.

c3.evidence: Nearly every American knows T-Mobile and its magenta brand, and it reports the highest NPS of the big three (46), but Verizon and AT&T are similarly well known, so it is not the single default choice.

c4.evidence: Its mission 'to be the best in the world at connecting customers to their world' and goal to become 'Famous for Network' are emphasised, but they are commercial rather than world-changing aims.

c6.evidence: “magenta, Un-carrier, fast 5G, value”: the impression is mostly positive, helped by network awards, but complaints about price and fee increases in 2024-2025 have taken some shine off.

c7.evidence: US connectivity is a large market and home broadband and satellite add growth, but wireless subscriptions grow slowly and do not ride a fast secular trend like AI.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into 5G home internet (8.5 million customers at end-2025), fiber through joint ventures, T-Satellite and business services, all adjacent to its core connectivity business.

m1.evidence: Srini Gopalan has set out a picture of an 'AI-enabled, data-informed, digital-first' T-Mobile 'Famous for Network', a clear strategy but not a transformational vision of the future.

m2.evidence: Gopalan is a career telecom executive who became CEO in November 2025 after a decade at Deutsche Telekom, not a founder.

m4.evidence: He links customer satisfaction to results ('NPS and churn are highly correlated') and stresses customer experience, but there is little public record yet of servant leadership toward employees.

m5.evidence: He inherits the Un-carrier culture built by John Legere and Mike Sievert and is pushing digital and AI tools, but the culture was not created by him.

m6.evidence: Gopalan is a marketing and commercial executive with a management degree from IIM Ahmedabad, not an engineer.

m7.evidence: There is no public controversy, but not enough record of his views beyond business performance to judge.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Srini Gopalan giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Gopalan is a low-key executive, unlike the flamboyant former CEO John Legere.

m9.evidence: He ran Deutsche Telekom's German business from 2020 to 2025, and under him T-Mobile grew Q2 2026 service revenue 9% and raised cash-flow guidance, but account additions fell 13% and churn rose.

m10.evidence: It is closing stores and moving sales online to cut costs ($108M of store-closure costs in Q2 2026), but it is not known for Bezos-style frugality.

c10.evidence: It connects 142.4 million customers to calls, internet and emergency services, a big benefit, but only in the US and in a service rivals also provide.

p2.evidence: Building and running a nationwide 5G network takes tens of billions of dollars of spectrum and about $10B of capital a year, and mobile connectivity is essential infrastructure.

f2.evidence: Revenue less cost of services and equipment rose from 58.7% of revenue in 2020 to 62.9% in 2025, and operating margin rose from 9.7% ($6,636M) to 20.7% ($18,279M).

f3.evidence: At June 30, 2026 it had $84,621M of short- and long-term debt against $2,825M of cash, about 3 times 2025 operating cash flow of $27,950M, though equity is a positive $56,265M.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $6,636M in 2020 to $18,279M in 2025 and operating cash flow from $8,640M to $27,950M.

v1.evidence: Independent tests now rank its network best (Ookla, Opensignal, P3, J.D. Power), a practical reason to choose it, but Verizon and AT&T remain close enough in many areas that it is not clearly best everywhere.

v2.evidence: It appeared on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For list in 2018, 2019, 2020, 2021 and 2024, but it is not a perennial top-ranked employer.

c5.evidence: If it vanished, its 142.4 million customers and businesses would lose phone and home internet service until they switched to Verizon or AT&T, though rivals could eventually replace it.
